mcqs.question: Which of the following best defines orbital overlap in the context of covalent bonding?

options.A: The interpenetration of atomic nuclei of two atoms
options.B: The interpenetration of electron clouds of atomic orbitals
options.C: The alignment of electron spins of two atoms
options.D: The merging of whole molecular orbitals of two molecules

mcqs.answer: The interpenetration of electron clouds of atomic orbitals
mcqs.explanation: Orbital overlap refers to the sharing of electron density when the electron clouds of two atomic orbitals come together, allowing a covalent bond to form. Overlap of nuclei or spins is not the basis of covalent bonding.

mcqs.question: In a carbon–carbon double bond (C=C), which type of bond is formed by the side‑by‑side overlap of p orbitals?
mcqs.explanation: A double bond consists of one sigma bond (head‑on overlap) and one pi bond, which arises from the side‑by‑side overlap of unhybridised p orbitals. The pi bond is responsible for the restricted rotation about the double bond.

mcqs.learning_point: Relate hybrid orbitals to molecular geometry
mcqs.question: Which hybridisation and geometry correctly describe the carbon atom in methane (CH₄)?
mcqs.explanation: In methane, the carbon atom undergoes sp³ hybridisation, forming four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals that arrange themselves tetrahedrally with bond angles of 109.5°, giving the observed geometry.

mcqs.learning_point: Understand limitations of simple valence-bond description
mcqs.question: Molecular oxygen (O₂) is experimentally found to be paramagnetic. Which limitation of the simple valence‑bond model fails to explain this observation?

options.A: The model does not consider orbital hybridisation
options.B: The model assumes all electrons in a bond are paired
options.C: The model ignores the involvement of d‑orbitals
options.D: The model treats all bonds as purely ionic

mcqs.answer: The model assumes all electrons in a bond are paired
mcqs.explanation: A simple valence‑bond description pairs all electrons in the O=O bond, predicting diamagnetism. In reality, two unpaired electrons occupy separate π* antibonding orbitals, giving O₂ its paramagnetic character, a feature the simple model cannot capture.

mcqs.question: A common misconception is that only s‑orbitals can overlap to form covalent bonds. Which statement correctly addresses this misconception?

options.A: Only s‑orbitals are capable of overlapping; p and d orbitals cannot.
options.B: p‑orbitals can also overlap, forming both sigma and pi bonds, while d‑orbitals may participate in bonding for transition elements.
options.C: d‑orbitals never participate in covalent bonding.
options.D: Orbital overlap is not required for covalent bond formation.

mcqs.answer: p‑orbitals can also overlap, forming both sigma and pi bonds, while d‑orbitals may participate in bonding for transition elements.
mcqs.explanation: Covalent bonds arise from the overlap of any compatible atomic orbitals—s, p, or d. Head‑on overlap of s or p orbitals gives sigma bonds; side‑by‑side overlap of p (or d) orbitals gives pi bonds. Hence the misconception is false.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds?

options.A: Sigma bonds are formed by head‑on (end‑to‑end) overlap of orbitals.
options.B: Pi bonds are formed by head‑on overlap of orbitals.
options.C: Sigma bonds allow free rotation about the bond axis, whereas pi bonds restrict rotation.
options.D: Pi bonds are always stronger than sigma bonds.

mcqs.answer: Sigma bonds are formed by head‑on (end‑to‑end) overlap of orbitals.
mcqs.explanation: Sigma bonds result from the direct, head‑on overlap of orbitals (s‑s, s‑p, or p‑p). Pi bonds arise from side‑by‑side overlap of parallel p (or d) orbitals. Sigma bonds permit rotation; pi bonds restrict it, and sigma bonds are generally stronger than pi bonds.

mcqs.learning_point: Relate hybrid orbitals to molecular geometry
mcqs.question: Which statement correctly matches a type of hybridisation with its characteristic bond angle?

options.A: sp hybridisation leads to bond angles of 109.5°
options.B: sp² hybridisation leads to bond angles of 120°
options.C: sp³ hybridisation leads to bond angles of 90°
options.D: dsp³ hybridisation leads to bond angles of 180°

mcqs.answer: sp² hybridisation leads to bond angles of 120°
mcqs.explanation: sp² hybridisation involves mixing one s and two p orbitals, producing three equivalent sp² hybrids that arrange in a trigonal planar geometry with 120° bond angles. sp gives 180°, sp³ gives 109.5°, and dsp³ gives 90°/120° depending on geometry, not 180°.

mcqs.learning_point: Understand limitations of simple valence-bond description
mcqs.question: Which of the following experimental observations cannot be explained by the simple valence‑bond model?

options.A: The linear geometry of carbon dioxide (CO₂)
options.D: The single bond length of hydrogen (H₂)

mcqs.explanation: The simple valence‑bond model predicts all electrons in O₂ to be paired, which would make it diamagnetic. The observed paramagnetism, due to two unpaired electrons in π* antibonding orbitals, requires molecular orbital theory, highlighting a limitation of the simple VB approach.
